en.title: Criminology and Security Studies: the whole course
en.short: What criminology and security studies is, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Criminology is the systematic study of crime, criminals, victims and the institutions that respond to crime. Security studies examines how people, organisations and states prevent harm, manage risk and protect what they value. The fields meet in policing, punishment, organised crime, cybercrime, terrorism and security governance. The course draws on sociology, law, psychology, political science and statistics, so you must read across disciplines and use evidence carefully.

Crime is both a legal and a social category. An act may be a crime in one country and not another, or at one time and not another. Criminologists study how laws are made and enforced, not only why people break them. Security studies asks whose security is protected, from what threat, and at what cost to rights. Where scholars disagree, the course sets out each view and its evidence.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree structures differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for length, awards and credit rules. In Nigeria, universities usually offer a four-year BSc in criminology, security studies or a combined programme, following benchmarks set by the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics, under the National Board for Technical Education, offer ND and HND awards in related fields; colleges of education offer the NCE. A master’s is usually one to two years, and a doctorate longer.

In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s is commonly three years and a master’s one year. In the United States, a bachelor’s is commonly four years and a master’s about two. South Africa commonly has a three-year bachelor’s, an honours year, then a master’s. Award names and the balance of law, methods and practice vary. Do not assume a module title means the same content elsewhere.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics come first: the discipline itself; crime, deviance and criminal law; police, courts and corrections; measuring crime and criminal statistics; social research foundations; basic statistics and data literacy; principles of security studies; ethics, human rights and accountability; and the history of criminology and penal reform.

Core topics build theory and institutions together. You study classical, rational choice and deterrence theories; biological and psychological theories; strain, anomie and subcultural theories; social learning, control and labelling theories; critical, conflict, feminist and green criminology; and developmental and life-course criminology. These are applied to environmental crime prevention and situational analysis, policing and law enforcement, courts, prosecution and sentencing, punishment, corrections and reintegration, victimology and victim services, organised crime and illicit markets, cybercrime and digital security, terrorism, political violence and counter-terrorism, and security governance, intelligence and surveillance. A core module on research design and data analysis teaches you to plan a study and interpret results.

Master’s topics deepen this: advanced criminological theory; advanced research methods and the dissertation; critical security studies, risk and resilience; and digital forensics and cybercrime investigation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by linking each claim to evidence. For every theory, write the question it asks, the mechanism it proposes, and the evidence that would support or weaken it. For every institution, ask what it is meant to do, what it does, and how we know. Use cases from your own country and elsewhere, but name the country and year.

Learn statistics by hand and with software. Practise reading tables, rates, graphs and confidence intervals. Never quote a crime figure without its source, year and definition. Use official sources such as national statistical offices, police reports, court reports and international surveys, and note their limits.

Read actively: summarise a chapter in your own words, then answer an exam question under time. In essays, state an argument, define terms, use evidence and address the strongest opposing view. Keep a glossary of legal and technical terms.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Common mistakes include treating a theory as a fact, or assuming that correlation proves causation. Students quote crime statistics without checking definitions, years or reporting practices, and compare figures across countries as if methods were identical.

Another mistake is describing an institution only by its official aims, without asking about practice or effects on rights. In theory essays, students list schools of thought without comparing them. In research work, they choose a topic that is too broad, ignore ethics approval, or report results without saying what they mean. Do not use a legal rule from one country as if it applied everywhere.

keyPoints: Criminology studies crime and the response to it; security studies studies how harm and risk are governed.
Crime is defined by law and shaped by society, so definitions vary by country and time.
Theories are tools: learn the question each asks, the mechanism it proposes and the evidence for it.
Every crime statistic needs its source, year and definition before you compare it.
Institutions should be judged by practice and effects, not only by official aims.
Degree length and awards vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook.

en.title: The Discipline of Criminology and Security Studies
en.short: What criminology and security studies are, their links to other fields, key terms and careers.

sections.heading: Two fields, one concern
sections.text: Criminology is the systematic study of crime, offenders, victims and the responses to crime, including prevention and control. It asks why crime happens, who is affected and what works. Security studies examines how people, groups and states are kept safe from threats. Its traditional focus was war and military power, but many scholars now include terrorism, cybercrime, organised crime and human security. Human security means safety from fear and want in daily life. The two fields overlap in prevention, governance and harm, but they are not the same. Criminology centres on crime; security studies centres on security, a contested idea.

sections.heading: Interdisciplinary links
sections.text: Both fields are interdisciplinary: they borrow methods and ideas from several subjects. Sociology shows how inequality, family, peers and community shape crime and safety. Law defines offences, police powers, procedure and rights; criminology studies how these rules work in practice. Psychology explains individual thinking, emotion and decision-making, including risk perception. Political science studies power, institutions, conflict and policy, which shape security governance. A small case shows the links. In a Nigerian market town, traders report repeated theft. Amina, a criminology student, studies the pattern; Chinedu, a psychology student, interviews shopkeepers about fear; a law student checks arrest powers; a political science student examines the local security committee. Together they ask what response is fair and effective.

sections.heading: Key terms and careers
sections.text: Key terms include theory (a set of ideas that explains why something happens), evidence-based policy (policy built on reliable research rather than guesswork), prevention (acting before harm occurs) and security governance (how the many public and private bodies manage security). Career paths vary by country. Graduates may work in police or prison services, courts, customs, immigration, private security, community safety, NGOs, research institutes or policy units. Some roles need further training or legal qualifications. Check current official requirements in your country before choosing a path.

keyPoints: Criminology studies crime, offenders, victims and responses; security studies studies threats to safety.
Security studies began with war and military power but now often includes terrorism, cybercrime and human security.
Both fields are interdisciplinary, drawing on sociology, law, psychology and political science.
Sociology explains social patterns; law sets rules and powers; psychology explains individual behaviour; political science explains governance and conflict.
Evidence-based policy uses reliable research to judge what works.
Career paths vary by country and may require further training, so check official requirements.

en.title: Crime, Deviance and Criminal Law
en.short: Legal, sociological and human rights views of crime, deviance and delinquency, and common law offence elements.

sections.heading: Three definitions
sections.text: Legal definitions treat crime as conduct that a state’s law forbids and punishes. The legality principle means no punishment without a prior, clear law. Sociological definitions treat crime as behaviour that breaks strong social norms; not every harmful act is illegal, and not every illegal act is widely condemned. Human rights definitions ask whether criminal law respects dignity, equality and fair trial, and whether states criminalise conduct that should be protected, such as peaceful expression. These views answer different questions.

sections.heading: Deviance and delinquency
sections.text: Deviance is behaviour that departs from norms; it may be criminal or not, and may be admired or condemned. Delinquency usually means offending by a minor (juvenile), but the age and procedures vary by country. A young person who steals is delinquent in legal usage; a person who dresses unusually is deviant but not criminal.

sections.heading: Elements of an offence
sections.text: In common law systems, an offence usually requires actus reus and mens rea. Actus reus is the prohibited act, or sometimes an omission where a duty exists, with any required result and causation. Mens rea is the mental element: intention, recklessness or negligence, depending on the offence. The two must concur, and the defendant must have legal capacity and no valid defence such as self-defence or duress. Some offences are strict liability, where mens rea need not be proved for part of the act. Definitions, ages and procedures vary by country; check the statute and courts of that jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Case and caution
sections.text: Case: Ada, 16, takes a phone from a market stall in Lagos, Nigeria, intending to keep it. In a common law analysis, the act of taking is actus reus; the intention to permanently deprive is mens rea; they concur. Whether she is a juvenile delinquent depends on Nigerian law’s age rules and court procedure, which the reader should check. If she honestly believed the phone was hers, mens rea may be absent.

keyPoints: Legal definitions see crime as conduct forbidden and punishable by state law.
Sociological definitions see crime as behaviour that breaks strong social norms.
Human rights definitions ask whether criminal law protects dignity, equality and fair trial.
Deviance is norm departure and need not be criminal; delinquency usually means juvenile offending.
Common law offences usually require actus reus, mens rea, concurrence and no valid defence.
Definitions, ages and procedures vary by country, so check the relevant statute and courts.

en.title: Criminal Justice Systems: Police, Courts and Corrections
en.short: Police, prosecution, courts and corrections; adversarial and inquisitorial models; discretion and accountability.

sections.heading: The main institutions
sections.text:
A criminal justice system is the set of institutions that respond to suspected crime. Police keep order, prevent and detect crime, investigate and arrest within legal powers. Prosecution decides whether to charge and presents the case in court. Courts decide guilt and sentence. Corrections carry out sentences, manage prisons and community sanctions, and support reintegration.

Each body has a different job, so checks between them matter.

sections.heading: Two court models
sections.text:
Adversarial and inquisitorial models describe court procedure; most countries mix them. In the adversarial model, used in Nigeria, England and Wales and other common-law countries, prosecution and defence present evidence before a neutral judge or jury. The judge is an umpire, and the prosecution must prove guilt.

In the inquisitorial model, associated with civil-law countries such as France, a judge or investigating magistrate may examine evidence and question witnesses actively, and a pre-trial file is important. The aim is an official inquiry, not only a contest.

sections.heading: Discretion and accountability
sections.text:
Discretion is lawful freedom to choose among options. Police choose whom to stop or arrest; prosecutors choose whether to charge; judges choose sentence; corrections choose parole or release. Discretion allows fair handling of individual cases but can produce bias or corruption. Accountability means explaining and reviewing those choices.

Courts, appeals, complaints bodies, prison inspectors, media and human rights law all play a part. In Nigeria, police and state prosecutors both handle criminal cases, and appeals and oversight bodies can review decisions. Rules differ by country, so check current law.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text:
Case: Amina, a trader in Kano, reports a stolen phone. Police investigate and arrest Musa. A prosecutor reviews the file and decides whether the evidence is enough to charge. In court, the prosecutor must prove the case; Musa may have a lawyer.

If convicted, the judge may impose a fine, community service or imprisonment, and corrections manage the sentence. If Amina thinks police acted improperly, she can complain to an oversight body.

keyPoints: Police investigate and arrest, prosecutors charge and present cases, courts decide guilt and sentence, and corrections carry out sentences.
Adversarial systems treat the trial as a contest before a neutral judge; inquisitorial systems expect active judicial inquiry.
Most real systems mix both models rather than matching one pure type.
Discretion at each stage allows individual fairness but creates risks of bias and corruption.
Accountability relies on appeals, oversight bodies, inspectors, media and human rights law.
Nigeria follows a common-law adversarial tradition, but police and state prosecutors both handle criminal cases; rules vary by country.

en.title: Measuring Crime and Criminal Statistics
en.short: Police records, victim and self-report surveys, the dark figure, bias and comparing crime rates.

sections.heading: Three main sources
sections.text: Police recorded crime counts offences that come to police attention and are entered in official records. Victim surveys ask a sample of people whether they experienced specified crimes in a set period, whether they reported them, and why not. Self-report surveys ask people, often young people, about offences they have committed. The three sources measure different things: police data measure recorded events, victim surveys measure victimisation in the sample, and self-report surveys measure admitted offending.

sections.heading: The dark figure
sections.text: The dark figure of crime is the gap between crimes committed and crimes recorded. It is not one fixed number. Victims may not report because they think the matter is minor, fear reprisals, distrust police or lack confidence in the justice system. Police may not record a report because they doubt it, classify it differently or face workload pressure. These are reporting bias and recording bias. They can change over time, so a rise in recorded crime may reflect more reporting or better recording rather than more crime.

sections.heading: Rates and comparison
sections.text: Crime rates make places with different populations easier to compare. The usual rate is per 100,000 people: crime rate = (number of recorded crimes ÷ population) × 100,000. Suppose Town A records 500 burglaries with a population of 250,000. Its rate is (500 ÷ 250,000) × 100,000 = 200 per 100,000. Town B records 300 burglaries with a population of 100,000, giving 300 per 100,000. Town B has the higher rate even though it has fewer burglaries.

sections.heading: Limits of comparison
sections.text: Comparison across places and years is limited. Legal definitions of offences differ between countries, as do counting rules and police practices. A country may change how it records crime, breaking the series. Victim surveys use different questions, samples and reference periods. Self-report surveys depend on honesty and memory. Population figures may be inaccurate. Always check the source, definition and year before comparing, and do not treat recorded crime as a complete count of crime.

keyPoints: Police recorded crime counts offences known to and recorded by police, not all crimes committed.
Victim surveys capture experiences of crime, including some incidents not reported to police.
Self-report surveys ask people about their own offending and are useful for hidden or minor offences.
The dark figure is the gap between crimes committed and crimes recorded; it varies by offence, place and time.
Reporting and recording bias mean official figures can rise or fall without real change in crime.
Crime rate per 100,000 = (number of recorded crimes ÷ population) × 100,000; comparisons need matching definitions and years.

en.title: Foundations of Social Research in Criminology
en.short: The research process in criminology: problems, literature, questions, sampling, measurement, data types and ethics.

sections.heading: From problem to question
sections.text: Social research is a planned way to answer a question about people, groups or institutions. It begins with a problem statement: a short account of what is unknown and why it matters for crime or security. A literature review then summarises what studies already show, so the student does not repeat work and can name a gap. From that gap come research questions: clear, narrow and answerable questions that guide the study. A good question names the group, the issue and the setting.

sections.heading: Sampling and measurement
sections.text: The population is everyone the study concerns; the sample is the smaller group studied. In probability sampling every member has a known chance of selection, as in simple random or stratified sampling. In non-probability sampling, such as convenience or snowball sampling, that chance is unknown; snowball sampling is useful for hidden groups. Measurement means deciding how each idea will be observed. An operational definition states how a concept such as 'reporting a theft' is recorded. A measure should be reliable (gives stable results) and valid (measures what it claims).

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text: Quantitative data are numbers, such as counts or scores; qualitative data are words, such as interview accounts. Many criminology studies mix both. Ethics protect participants and the public. Researchers need approval from an ethics committee, informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality and anonymity, and they must avoid harm. Deception is allowed only rarely, with strong justification and a debrief afterwards.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Amina, a first-year student in Kano, Nigeria, notices that market traders seldom report theft. Her problem statement asks why. After a literature review, her question is: 'What stops traders at a Kano market from reporting theft to the police?' The stall population is 400; she takes a systematic sample of 80, choosing every fifth stall after a random start (400 ÷ 80 = 5). She interviews 20 traders and surveys all 80, measuring reporting with yes or no answers. She obtains consent and keeps names out of her notes.

keyPoints: A problem statement says what is unknown and why it matters.
A literature review shows what is already known and where the gap is.
Research questions should be clear, narrow and answerable.
Probability sampling gives every member a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling does not.
A reliable measure gives stable results; a valid measure measures the intended concept.
Ethical research needs consent, confidentiality, no harm and ethics approval.

en.title: Basic Statistics and Data Literacy for Criminology
en.short: Variables, measurement levels, tables, graphs, averages, variation, rates and correlation versus causation.

sections.heading: Variables and levels
sections.text: A variable is any characteristic that can differ between cases, such as age, offence type or victimisation. Its level of measurement limits what you can calculate. Nominal variables are named categories with no order (burglary, robbery). Ordinal variables are ordered but gaps are not equal (low, medium, high fear). Interval variables have equal gaps but no true zero (temperature, some test scores). Ratio variables have equal gaps and a true zero, so ratios make sense (number of offences, age).

sections.heading: Tables and graphs
sections.text: A frequency table lists each value or class and its count. For categories use a bar chart; for continuous data grouped into classes use a histogram. Percentages show share of a total; rates show events per fixed population, often per 100,000. Example: 30 burglaries in a town of 150,000 is (30 ÷ 150,000) × 100,000 = 20 per 100,000. A second town with 45 burglaries and 300,000 people has 15 per 100,000, so its rate is lower despite more offences.

sections.heading: Averages and variation
sections.text: An average summarises the centre. The mean adds all values and divides by the count; the median is the middle value when ordered; the mode is the most frequent. Variation describes spread: range, variance and standard deviation. For reports 2, 4, 4, 6, 9: mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5, median = 4, mode = 4, range = 9 − 2 = 7. The standard deviation is roughly the typical distance from the mean.

sections.heading: Correlation and cause
sections.text: Correlation measures how two variables move together. Pearson r runs from −1 to +1; near 0 means little linear association. Correlation does not prove causation. A causal claim needs time order, a plausible mechanism and control of confounders, which are other factors that affect both variables. Example: ice-cream sales and burglary may correlate because both rise in warm months; heat is a confounder, not proof that ice cream causes crime.

keyPoints: A variable is a characteristic that varies; its level of measurement decides which summaries are valid.
Nominal data are named categories, ordinal data are ordered, interval data have equal gaps, and ratio data have a true zero.
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; median = middle ordered value; mode = most frequent value.
Rate per 100,000 = (number of events ÷ population) × 100,000.
Correlation r runs from −1 to +1 and measures linear association, not causation.
Causation requires time order, a mechanism and control of confounders.

en.title: Principles of Security Studies
en.short: Security, threat, risk and vulnerability; national and human security; levels of analysis; asset protection.

sections.heading: Security and harm
sections.text: Security is a condition in which important values, people and assets are protected from serious harm. It is not simply the absence of danger; it is the management of danger to an acceptable level. A threat is a person, group, event or condition with the potential to cause harm. Risk is the chance that harm will occur and how serious it would be. Vulnerability is a weakness that makes harm more likely or worse. A locked gate reduces vulnerability; a known thief is a threat; the risk depends on both.

sections.heading: National and human security
sections.text: National security concerns the state: its territory, sovereignty, institutions and citizens. It is often linked to military defence, intelligence and border control. Human security shifts the focus to individuals and communities, especially freedom from fear and freedom from want. The two can support each other, but they can also conflict. A government may restrict movement for state security while increasing insecurity for local people. Analysts therefore ask whose security is being protected.

sections.heading: Levels of analysis
sections.text: Security can be studied at four levels. Individual security concerns one person’s safety and rights. Community security concerns families, neighbourhoods, ethnic or religious groups and shared spaces. State security concerns public order and national institutions. International security concerns relations between states and global problems such as war, terrorism and organised crime. The levels interact: a local dispute can become a national or international issue.

sections.heading: Asset protection and management
sections.text: Asset protection means identifying what must be safeguarded, then reducing threat, risk and vulnerability through layered controls. Security management is the planning, organising and review of those controls. Case: a university in Accra stores exam scripts in a room with a broken lock. The threat is theft by an insider; the vulnerability is weak access control; the risk is high because loss would be serious. Controls include a strong lock, access records and regular checks. Management reviews whether the controls work.

keyPoints: Security is the protection of people, values and assets from serious harm to an acceptable level.
A threat is a potential source of harm; risk combines likelihood and impact; vulnerability is a weakness that increases harm.
National security protects the state, while human security protects individuals and communities.
The individual, community, state and international levels interact and should be analysed together.
Asset protection reduces risk through layered controls after identifying assets, threats and vulnerabilities.
Security management plans, organises and reviews those controls.

en.title: Ethics, Human Rights and Accountability
en.short: Professional ethics, human rights, use of force, corruption, accountability and research consent.

sections.heading: Professional ethics
sections.text: Professional ethics are the rules and values that guide how people in a profession act. In policing, private security and corrections, ethics means integrity, impartiality, respect for dignity and lawful conduct. Officers have power over others, so codes of conduct, training and supervision matter. Corrections staff must treat prisoners humanely; security staff must not act as police unless the law allows it.

sections.heading: Human rights and force
sections.text: Human rights are basic entitlements held by every person, such as life, liberty, fair trial and freedom from torture. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states them; later treaties make some binding on states that ratify them. Use of force must be lawful, necessary and proportionate. Necessary means no less harmful option will work. Proportionate means the harm is not excessive for the aim. Firearms are a last resort. A handcuffed suspect who is not resisting should not be struck.

sections.heading: Corruption and accountability
sections.text: Corruption is the misuse of entrusted power for private gain, including bribes, extortion and abuse of office. Accountability means being answerable for decisions. It needs clear rules, records, complaint channels, independent oversight and courts. Case: Amina, a trader, is stopped by an officer who demands money and threatens arrest. She reports it. A complaint unit records the allegation, collects witness statements and reviews body-camera footage. The officer faces disciplinary and possible criminal action. Without records and independent review, such abuse is hard to prove.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: In criminological research, informed consent means participants understand the study, its risks and benefits, and agree freely. They may withdraw. Confidentiality means protecting identities and data. Researchers should collect only needed data, store it securely and report results without naming people. Confidentiality has limits: if a participant reveals a serious immediate danger, the researcher may have a duty to report, following ethics approval and local law.

keyPoints: Professional ethics require integrity, lawful conduct and respect for dignity in policing, security and corrections.
Human rights are basic entitlements of every person; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is a key statement.
Use of force must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, with firearms as a last resort.
Corruption is misuse of entrusted power for private gain; accountability needs records, complaints, oversight and courts.
Informed consent means voluntary, informed agreement, and participants may withdraw.
Confidentiality protects identities and data, but may have legal limits when serious harm is threatened.

en.title: History of Criminology and Penal Reform
en.short: Enlightenment classical school, Lombroso’s positivism, penal reform and colonial readings.

sections.heading: Enlightenment and classical school
sections.text: The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century European movement that stressed reason and limits on arbitrary power. Cesare Beccaria, in On Crimes and Punishments (1764), argued punishment should be certain, swift and proportionate, and torture and excessive severity were unjust and ineffective. Jeremy Bentham added a utilitarian case: law should increase happiness, and punishment is a cost justified by future crime prevented. This is the classical school: people are rational choosers, so the focus is law and deterrence, not the offender’s body.

sections.heading: Positivism and Lombroso
sections.text: Positivism looked for causes of crime in the individual and society, using observation and measurement. Cesare Lombroso, in L’uomo delinquente (1876), claimed that some criminals were 'born criminals’ marked by physical stigmata. His methods and conclusions are now rejected as biased and unscientific. His importance is historical: he shifted attention from the act to the offender and encouraged later biological and psychological work. Treat his claims critically.

sections.heading: Penal reform
sections.text: Classical ideas fed penal reform. Reformers attacked torture, arbitrary imprisonment and public executions, and urged written codes, fixed sentences and prisons meant to correct rather than merely destroy. Bentham designed the panopticon, a prison with a central watchtower, as a model of inspection and control. Reform was uneven: it depended on state capacity, religion, politics and public opinion. Harsh corporal and capital punishment continued in many places after reform laws.

sections.heading: Colonial and regional contexts
sections.text: Criminology’s history is not only European. Colonial powers exported codes, police and prisons to Asia, Africa and the Caribbean, often for control. In colonial Africa, criminal law and prisons formed part of racial and labour control, and customary authorities were reshaped for colonial ends. After independence, many states kept these structures. Imagine Amina, a student in Kano, comparing Nigeria’s prison and correctional laws with Britain’s: she must ask who wrote the law, who was policed and who was protected. Answers differ by country, so check local histories.

keyPoints: The Enlightenment classical school treated offenders as rational and stressed certain, proportionate punishment.
Beccaria and Bentham influenced penal reform by attacking torture and excessive severity.
Lombroso’s positivism claimed born criminals had physical stigmata, a view now rejected.
Positivism shifted attention from the act to the offender but carried bias.
Penal reform was uneven and often coexisted with harsh punishment.
Criminology’s history must be read with colonial and regional contexts because legal and prison systems were exported and adapted.

en.title: Classical, Rational Choice and Deterrence Theories
en.short: Beccaria, Bentham, expected utility, general and specific deterrence, evidence limits and policy.

sections.heading: Classical foundations
sections.text: Cesare Beccaria, in On Crimes and Punishments (1764), and Jeremy Bentham built the classical school on the idea that people choose crime when it seems advantageous. Beccaria argued that punishment should be proportionate, certain and swift, and no more severe than needed to prevent crime. Bentham’s utilitarianism judged laws by their tendency to produce the greatest happiness, weighing pain against pleasure. Both treated the offender as a reasoning person, not as someone driven by innate wickedness.

sections.heading: Rational choice and expected utility
sections.text: Rational choice theory extends this: offenders weigh expected gains against expected costs, though with limited time and information. Expected utility is the value of an outcome multiplied by its probability. Suppose a gain of 10,000 units, success probability 0.8, and a fine of 20,000 if caught with probability 0.2. Expected gain = 0.8 × 10,000 = 8,000. Expected cost = 0.2 × 20,000 = 4,000. Net expected utility = 4,000. If detection probability rises to 0.5, expected gain = 0.5 × 10,000 = 5,000, expected cost = 10,000 and net = −5,000.

sections.heading: General and specific deterrence
sections.text: General deterrence aims to stop people who have not offended by public example. Specific deterrence aims to stop a punished offender reoffending. Deterrence depends on certainty, severity and speed of punishment. Research often finds certainty more important than severity, but evidence is mixed and hard to isolate from other effects such as incapacitation and informal sanctions.

sections.heading: Limits and policy implications
sections.text: Deterrence evidence has limits. Offenders may not know the law or may discount future punishment. Harsh sentences may increase reoffending and prison populations. Crime prevention should therefore combine proportionate, certain and swift responses with situational measures that reduce opportunity. Policy should not assume that longer sentences automatically deter.

keyPoints: Beccaria and Bentham treat offenders as rational choosers and punishment as a means of prevention.
Expected utility = probability of outcome × value of outcome; net expected utility = expected gain − expected cost.
General deterrence targets potential offenders; specific deterrence targets the punished offender.
Certainty and speed of punishment often matter more than severity, though evidence is mixed.
Deterrence research struggles to separate deterrence from incapacitation and informal sanctions.
Proportionate, certain and swift punishment plus situational prevention is safer policy than relying on harsh sentences.

en.title: Biological and Psychological Theories of Crime
en.short: Early positivism, biosocial and genetic research, neurology, personality, psychopathy, mental disorder and ethics.

sections.heading: Early positivism
sections.text:
Early positivism looked for crime’s causes in the body. Cesare Lombroso claimed some offenders were 'born criminals', marked by atavism: physical features he read as signs of an earlier evolutionary stage. Enrico Ferri and Raffaele Garofalo built on such ideas.

Flaws were serious. Studies lacked control groups, used biased prison samples, and confused poverty with biology. The theory was deterministic and helped justify eugenics and racist policies.

sections.heading: Modern biosocial views
sections.text:
Biosocial criminology treats biology and social life as interacting. Heritability is the share of variation in a trait, within a population, linked to genetic differences; it is not an individual’s destiny. Twin and adoption studies suggest modest heritability for some antisocial behaviour. Gene-environment interaction means a variant may matter only with adversity, such as maltreatment. Some studies report this for a MAOA variant, but findings are debated.

Neurological work links self-control and planning to the prefrontal cortex, and threat response to the amygdala. Head injury and lead exposure show associations, not causation.

sections.heading: Personality and disorder
sections.text:
Psychological explanations focus on personality and mental state. Traits such as impulsivity, sensation seeking and low empathy predict antisocial behaviour statistically. Psychopathy is a personality construct, measured by the Hare Psychopathy Checklist. It combines callous affect, manipulation, impulsivity and antisocial conduct. It is not psychosis, and it is not a diagnosis of violence.

Mental disorder alone is a weak predictor of violence. Substance misuse and delusions raise risk; people with mental disorder are also more often victims. Consider Chidi, 19, with a head injury, childhood neglect and heavy drinking. Assessment should list these interacting risks, not label him a born criminal.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits
sections.text:
Evidence is correlational. Effect sizes are modest, and group findings cannot be applied to one person (ecological fallacy). Risk markers are not causes.

Ethical limits matter. Biological claims have supported eugenics and racial stigma. Genetic and brain data raise privacy and consent issues. Prediction tools produce false positives. Courts should not treat biology as destiny, and punishment should remain proportionate.

keyPoints: Early positivism linked crime to body features but lacked controls and was biased and deterministic.
Heritability describes population variation, not an individual’s fixed fate.
Genes interact with environments; a variant may raise risk only under adversity such as maltreatment.
Neurological and psychological findings are probabilistic risk markers; group results cannot be applied to one person.
Psychopathy is a personality construct, not psychosis, and mental disorder alone weakly predicts violence.
Biological evidence raises stigma, privacy and prediction ethics; courts should not treat it as destiny.

en.title: Strain, Anomie and Subcultural Theories
en.short: This summary covers Durkheim, Merton, Agnew, Cohen and Cloward and Ohlin on strain, subcultures and policy.

sections.heading: Durkheim and anomie
sections.text: Durkheim used anomie for a state of weak social regulation, where shared norms lose their force. He treated crime as normal in every society, but anomie signals weak regulation, not weak integration. His point is social: rapid change or weak rules can leave people without clear standards.

sections.heading: Merton’s strain theory
sections.text: Merton (1938) argued that society teaches goals such as success but blocks legitimate means for some groups. The gap between goals and means is strain. He listed five adaptations: conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion. Conformity accepts both goals and means. Innovation, using illegitimate means, is often linked to property crime.

sections.heading: Agnew and subcultures
sections.text: Agnew’s general strain theory (1992) broadened strain to failure to achieve goals, loss of valued things and negative treatment. Strain produces anger and frustration, which can lead to crime as coping, across social classes. Cohen (1955) argued that working-class boys faced status frustration and formed delinquent subcultures that inverted mainstream values. Cloward and Ohlin (1960) added differential opportunity: access to illegitimate means varies, producing criminal, conflict and retreatist subcultures. These theories extend Merton rather than replace him.

sections.heading: Policy implications
sections.text: Policy implications include widening legitimate opportunity through education, training and youth employment, supporting schools and families, and reducing harsh or humiliating treatment by institutions. Subcultural theories also point to status, belonging and community programmes. Evaluations vary, so these are theory-informed directions, not guaranteed fixes. Case: two school leavers in a city with few formal jobs, Ada and Musa, face blocked goals. Ada finds a training scheme; Musa joins a group that rewards theft. Strain theory reads Musa’s path as innovation, while subcultural theory asks whether the group supplies status and illegitimate opportunity.

keyPoints: Durkheim’s anomie means weak social regulation, not simply crime.
Merton’s strain is the gap between cultural goals and legitimate means.
Merton’s adaptations are conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion.
Agnew’s general strain theory adds negative treatment and loss, and links strain to anger and coping.
Cohen explains delinquent subcultures as a response to status frustration, while Cloward and Ohlin stress unequal access to illegitimate opportunity.
Policy should widen legitimate opportunity and reduce humiliating treatment, but effects vary.

en.title: Social Learning, Control and Labelling Theories
en.short: Sutherland, Akers, Hirschi and labelling theory, with strengths and criticisms.

sections.heading: Learning crime
sections.text:
Sutherland’s differential association (1939) holds that criminal behaviour is learned in intimate groups. People learn both techniques and definitions: motives, attitudes and justifications that make breaking the law seem acceptable. Crime follows when definitions favourable to law-breaking outweigh unfavourable ones.

Akers extended this as social learning theory, keeping differential association and definitions and adding differential reinforcement (rewards and punishments that follow behaviour) and imitation. Behaviour is repeated when it pays off socially.

sections.heading: Control and bonds
sections.text:
Hirschi, in Causes of Delinquency (1969), asks why most people do not offend. He names four social bonds: attachment to others, commitment to conventional goals, involvement in activities, and belief in the rules. Weak bonds free a person to offend.

Gottfredson and Hirschi (1990) moved to self-control, said to form in early childhood through parental supervision, and to combine with opportunity to produce crime.

sections.heading: Labelling
sections.text:
Labelling theory shifts attention from the offender to the reaction. Tannenbaum (1938) described the dramatisation of evil, where a minor act is made into a defining feature of the person. Becker (1963) argued that deviance is not a quality of the act but a consequence of rules and sanctions applied by others. Moral entrepreneurs press for those rules. Lemert separated primary deviance from secondary deviance, the latter shaped by the label.

A boy cautioned for a small theft may return to school. One labelled a thief may be pushed towards the company of other offenders.

sections.heading: Strengths and criticisms
sections.text:
Learning theory explains peer and family influence. Control theory explains conformity. Labelling explains selective enforcement and the effects of official reaction.

Criticisms: differential association is hard to test and its key terms are vague. Social learning risks circularity when reinforcement is inferred from the behaviour it is meant to explain. Hirschi’s bonds are measured unevenly, and self-control theory is accused of tautology and of ignoring structure. Labelling says little about the first causes of acts, and its predicted effects are not always found.

keyPoints: Differential association says crime is learned in intimate groups, including techniques and definitions.
Akers keeps Sutherland’s differential association and definitions and adds differential reinforcement and imitation.
Hirschi’s four bonds are attachment, commitment, involvement and belief; weak bonds allow offending.
Gottfredson and Hirschi link low self-control, formed early in life, with opportunity to crime.
Becker argues deviance is a consequence of rules and reactions, not a quality of the act itself.
Main criticisms are vague or circular concepts and neglect of structural causes.

en.title: Critical, Conflict, Feminist and Green Criminology
en.short: Marxist, conflict, feminist and green criminology: how power shapes law, crime and victimisation.

sections.heading: Conflict and Marxist criminology
sections.text: Conflict criminology sees society as a contest between groups with unequal power. Law is not neutral: it tends to protect dominant interests, and crime is a label applied unevenly. Marxist criminology, rooted in Marx, argues that capitalism produces inequality, competition and egoism, and that criminal law guards property and ruling-class interests. Crimes of the powerful, such as unsafe workplaces or tax evasion, are often under-policed, while street crime is punished. Not all conflict theorists are Marxists, and later writers stress that law can also restrain powerful groups.

sections.heading: Feminist criminology
sections.text: Feminist criminology asks how gender, especially patriarchy, shapes crime, law and victimisation. It criticises older criminology for studying men and treating male behaviour as normal. It examines women’s offending, often linked to poverty, abuse and caring duties; sexual and domestic violence; and double standards in policing and sentencing. Liberal, radical and socialist feminist strands disagree about causes and remedies, while intersectional work shows that class, race and gender combine. Power relations shape who is believed, who is protected and who is punished.

sections.heading: Green criminology and power
sections.text:
Green criminology studies harm to the environment, animals and ecosystems. It includes illegal dumping but also legal harms, such as pollution permitted by weak regulation. It asks who gains and who bears the cost, linking environmental harm to corporate and state power. Environmental justice research shows that poor communities often face the greatest exposure. Victimisation may be direct, through illness, or indirect, through lost livelihoods and damaged land.

Hypothetical case: a firm dumps drilling waste near a fishing village in the Niger Delta. If a permit makes it legal, it is still an ecological and social harm. Conflict criminology asks who wrote the permit. Feminist criminology asks who does the extra care work when children fall ill. Green criminology names the damaged water and fish. Law, power and harm can diverge.

keyPoints: Conflict criminology treats law and crime as products of unequal power between social groups.
Marxist criminology links crime and law under capitalism to class inequality and property interests.
Feminist criminology shows how patriarchy and gender shape offending, victimisation and criminal justice responses.
Intersectional analysis adds class and race to gender.
Green criminology studies environmental harm whether or not it is legally defined as crime.
Environmental justice highlights unequal exposure of poor communities to harm.

en.title: Developmental and Life-Course Criminology
en.short: Age-crime curve, Moffitt’s pathways, Sampson and Laub, risk factors and desistance.

sections.heading: Age and crime
sections.text: Developmental and life-course criminology studies how offending changes with age and how early experiences and later events shape that path. The age-crime curve is the aggregate pattern in which offending rises through childhood and adolescence, peaks in the late teens or early twenties, then falls. It varies by offence, place and cohort, and it is a summary, not a prediction for every person.

sections.heading: Moffitt’s pathways
sections.text: Moffitt (1993) proposed two pathways. Life-course persistent offenders are a small group who begin antisocial behaviour in childhood and continue into adulthood. Moffitt links this to neurodevelopmental deficits interacting with criminogenic environments. Adolescent-limited offenders are a larger group who begin in adolescence and mostly stop in early adulthood, as the maturity gap (biologically mature but not yet granted adult status) closes and adult roles replace peer approval. The taxonomy is influential but contested; some studies find more varied pathways.

sections.heading: Life-course control
sections.text: Sampson and Laub’s age-graded theory of informal social control holds that bonds to family, school and work restrain offending. Childhood disadvantage creates continuity, but turning points such as marriage or a stable job can redirect lives. Their reanalysis of the Gluecks’ longitudinal data supported this. The theory stresses continuity and change; one event does not guarantee desistance.

sections.heading: Risk and desistance
sections.text: Risk factors raise the probability of offending; protective factors reduce or buffer that risk. They operate across individual, family, school, peer and community domains and often accumulate. They are probabilistic, not deterministic. Desistance is the process by which offending declines and stops, not just one decision. It is linked to ageing, social bonds, new identities and agency. Example: Amina, 15, joins a peer group and starts shoplifting. At 19 a stable job and a supportive older sister give structure and a new identity; she stops. The case shows turning points and agency, not a fixed criminal type.

keyPoints: The age-crime curve rises in adolescence, peaks in the late teens or early twenties, then declines.
Moffitt distinguishes life-course persistent from adolescent-limited pathways.
Sampson and Laub stress age-graded informal social control and turning points.
Risk factors raise and protective factors lower or buffer the probability of offending.
Desistance is a process, not a single event.

en.title: Environmental Crime Prevention and Situational Analysis
en.short: Routine activity, hot spots, situational prevention, CPTED, displacement and evaluation.

sections.heading: Routine activity and patterns
sections.text:
Routine activity theory, from Cohen and Felson (1979), says crime needs three things to meet in time and place: a motivated offender, a suitable target, and no capable guardian. A guardian may be a person, a lock, a camera or a neighbour.

Crime pattern theory adds that offenders move through awareness spaces: nodes they use, paths between them, and edges where areas meet. This helps explain why crime clusters near transport stops, markets and schools.

sections.heading: Hot spots and mapping
sections.text:
Hot spot analysis maps crime to find small areas or short periods with high counts. Analysts use point maps, grid counts, kernel density estimation and near repeat analysis.

A hot spot is not proof of a cause. It may reflect more people, more reporting, or police activity. Crime pattern analysis links hot spots to everyday routes and nodes. It guides patrol and design, but must be checked against local data and civil rights concerns.

sections.heading: Situational prevention and CPTED
sections.text:
Situational crime prevention, associated with Ronald Clarke, reduces opportunities rather than changing offenders. It increases the effort and risk of crime, reduces rewards, reduces provocation and removes excuses. Examples are locks, lighting, clear sight lines, and reception desks.

CPTED, crime prevention through environmental design, uses design to reduce opportunity. Its principles include natural surveillance, access control, territorial reinforcement and maintenance. These ideas draw on Jane Jacobs and Oscar Newman. A well-lit market entrance with one gate and a visible attendant is a case.

sections.heading: Displacement and evaluation
sections.text:
Prevention can displace crime to another place, time, target, method or offender. It can also produce diffusion of benefits, where nearby areas gain. Evaluation needs a comparison area and before and after measures, not just a fall in one site. Random assignment is strongest.

Good studies measure displacement and diffusion, and check whether crime fell or only moved. Suppose a Lagos campus adds a gate and guard at a hostel path. If theft falls there but rises at the back fence, the net gain may be small.

keyPoints: Routine activity theory says crime needs a motivated offender, a suitable target and no capable guardian in the same time and place.
Crime pattern theory links offending to nodes, paths and edges in an offender’s awareness space.
Hot spot analysis maps concentrations of crime, but hot spots may reflect reporting or policing as well as offending.
Situational prevention cuts opportunity by raising effort and risk, lowering rewards, reducing provocation and removing excuses.
CPTED uses natural surveillance, access control, territorial reinforcement and maintenance to reduce crime opportunity.
Evaluation must test displacement and diffusion of benefits with comparison areas and before and after measures.

en.title: Policing and Law Enforcement
en.short: Models of policing, community and problem-oriented approaches, discretion, force, oversight and Nigeria comparisons.

sections.heading: Models of policing
sections.text: Policing is the whole task of keeping order, preventing crime and serving the public; law enforcement is the narrower job of applying the law. The policing by consent model, linked to Sir Robert Peel’s London force of 1829, holds that officers need public acceptance and should use minimum force. Systems in continental Europe often stress state authority and central control instead. Other models include professional policing, which stresses trained, efficient forces, and intelligence-led policing, which directs resources by risk, as well as community and problem-oriented policing.

sections.heading: Community and problem-oriented
sections.text: Community policing builds consultation, partnership and regular contact between officers and residents. Problem-oriented policing, set out by Herman Goldstein in 1979, goes further: police identify recurring problems and address their causes using the SARA cycle (Scanning, Analysis, Response, Assessment). Example: in a Kano market, trader Amina reports repeated phone thefts. Instead of only arresting one suspect, officers map the hotspots, work with market leaders on lighting and stalls, and review theft reports after two months.

sections.heading: Discretion and force
sections.text: Discretion is an officer’s power, within law and policy, to choose among possible actions: to warn, mediate, stop, arrest or refer. Law, policy, seriousness, evidence, victim wishes, resources and, unavoidably, bias shape it. Because discretion is unavoidable, rules and supervision matter. Use of force must be legal, necessary and proportionate, and is governed by the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms (1990). Deadly force is a last resort to protect life.

sections.heading: Accountability and comparison
sections.text: Accountability has internal and external sides. Internally, forces use discipline, training and complaints units; externally, courts, police authorities, independent inspectors, legislatures and media scrutinise them. Nigeria has one national force under the 1999 Constitution, overseen by the Police Service Commission, with the Public Complaints Commission as an ombudsman. In England and Wales, the Independent Office for Police Conduct investigates serious cases. After the 2020 #EndSARS protests against the Special Anti-Robbery Squad, Nigerian states set up judicial panels of inquiry. Centralised and decentralised systems each trade consistency against local responsiveness.

keyPoints: Policing is broader than law enforcement: it includes order maintenance, prevention and service.
The policing by consent model, linked to Peel’s 1829 London force, relies on public acceptance and minimum force.
Problem-oriented policing uses the SARA cycle to address the causes of recurring problems, not just single incidents.
Discretion is unavoidable, so law, policy, supervision and training matter.
Use of force must be legal, necessary and proportionate; the UN Basic Principles (1990) set the standard.
Accountability combines internal discipline with external oversight; Nigeria’s single national force is checked by the Police Service Commission and the courts.

en.title: Courts, Prosecution and Sentencing
en.short: Prosecution, bail and remand, plea bargaining, sentencing theories, disparities, restorative justice and fair trial rights.

sections.heading: Prosecution and trial
sections.text: Prosecution is the process by which a public authority brings a criminal charge in court. Courts may be adversarial, where two parties argue before a judge, or inquisitorial, where a judge investigates. Most African countries inherited one model from their colonial rulers, and some systems mix elements of both. The prosecutor should disclose evidence and must prove guilt to the required standard. The accused has a right to a lawyer, though access varies by country.

sections.heading: Bail, remand and pleas
sections.text: Bail releases an accused person before trial, sometimes with a surety (a person who guarantees the accused will attend trial) or conditions. Remand is detention while awaiting trial. Bail is favoured because the accused is presumed innocent, but courts weigh flight risk, witness danger and reoffending. Plea bargaining is an agreement in which the accused pleads guilty for a lesser charge or sentencing concession. It must be voluntary, informed and approved by the court. Nigeria’s Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015 provides for plea bargaining in federal courts and the Federal Capital Territory; state laws differ.

sections.heading: Sentencing theories
sections.text: Sentencing aims are retribution (punishment deserved), deterrence (preventing future crime), incapacitation (removing the offender from society), rehabilitation (reforming the offender) and reparation or restoration (repairing harm). Most systems combine them. A sentence may be a fine, probation, community service, imprisonment or, in some countries, death. The judge usually has discretion, guided by statute and precedent.

sections.heading: Disparities, restoration and rights
sections.text: Sentencing disparities occur when similar offenders receive different sentences because of bias, geography, wealth or court resources. Restorative justice brings victim, offender and community together to repair harm; it suits some cases but not all. Fair trial rights include presumption of innocence, counsel, impartial and public hearing, trial within a reasonable time, and appeal. These appear in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 14, and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, Article 7. Suppose Ada, a trader in Enugu, is charged with theft. Bail keeps her out of detention before trial, and legal aid helps her defend herself; both support the presumption of innocence in practice.

keyPoints: Bail is release before trial; remand is detention while awaiting trial.
Bail is favoured by the presumption of innocence but courts weigh flight risk and witness danger.
Plea bargains must be voluntary, informed and approved by the court.
Sentencing theories are retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation and restoration.
Restorative justice repairs harm through victim, offender and community processes.
Fair trial rights include presumption of innocence, counsel, impartial hearing and appeal.

en.title: Punishment, Corrections and Reintegration
en.short: Justifications for punishment, prisons, probation, parole, rehabilitation and abolition debates.

sections.heading: Justifying punishment
sections.text:
Punishment is a deliberate penalty imposed by the state for a wrong. Five standard justifications are retribution (deserved suffering), deterrence (preventing future offences by the punished person or others), incapacitation (removing the ability to offend), rehabilitation (changing the offender) and restoration (repairing harm to victims and communities). Most systems mix them, though they can conflict: a harsh deterrent sentence may hinder rehabilitation.

Sentencing law and practice differ by country. Some legal systems encourage non-custodial measures (penalties served outside prison), but courts still use imprisonment widely. Students should check the current law of their own jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Prisons, probation and parole
sections.text:
Corrections is the umbrella term for prisons, probation, parole and related services. Prisons hold people awaiting trial and those sentenced. Overcrowding happens when the number of prisoners exceeds capacity, often because of pre-trial detention, long sentences and limited alternatives. It worsens health, violence, sanitation and access to work or education. Conditions vary widely between countries and institutions.

Probation is a community sentence served instead of prison, usually with conditions and supervision. Parole is the early release of a prisoner after part of the sentence, under supervision. Both aim to manage risk and support resettlement, but they depend on trained staff and fair decisions.

sections.heading: Effects and reintegration
sections.text:
Imprisonment removes liberty and often separates people from family, work and housing. It can cause psychological harm, expose people to criminal networks and leave a stigma that makes reoffending more likely. These are sometimes called the pains of imprisonment and the criminogenic effects of prison.

Rehabilitation means purposeful work, education, treatment and skills. Reintegration means helping a released person rejoin society through family contact, housing, employment and community support. A short hypothetical case: Amina, a first offender in Kano, Nigeria, receives probation with community service instead of a short prison term; she keeps her job and family ties. The outcome depends on supervision and the local context.

sections.heading: Abolition and reform
sections.text: Reformists accept prisons but seek decarceration (reducing the number of people in prison), humane conditions, alternatives and independent oversight. Abolitionists argue that prisons do not reliably reduce crime and cause serious harm, so society should replace them with community-based responses. Critics of abolition ask what should be done about serious violence. The debate is normative and empirical, and evidence and values both matter.

keyPoints: Punishment is justified by retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation and restoration, and these aims can conflict.
Prison overcrowding is driven by high admissions and limited capacity, and it harms health, safety and rehabilitation.
Probation is a community sentence instead of prison; parole is supervised early release from prison.
Imprisonment can cause psychological harm, family disruption and stigma, which may increase reoffending.
Reintegration requires practical support such as housing, work, treatment and family contact.
Reformists seek to improve and reduce prisons; abolitionists seek to replace them, and the debate turns on evidence and values.

en.title: Victimology, Victim Rights and Victim Services
en.short: Victim typologies, fear of crime, repeat and secondary victimisation, rights, support and surveys.

sections.heading: Victim typologies
sections.text:
Victimology studies people harmed by crime. Victim typologies group victims by vulnerability or conduct. Benjamin Mendelsohn ranked victims by culpability, from innocent to fully responsible. Hans von Hentig listed personal characteristics linked to risk, such as youth, old age, isolation or mental illness. Stephen Schafer focused on functional responsibility, including provocative or precipitative behaviour. These are ideal types, not moral verdicts, and must not be used to blame victims.

In the justice process a victim may report the crime, give evidence and, where the law allows, make a victim impact statement. That role varies by country.

sections.heading: Fear and victimisation
sections.text:
Fear of crime is the emotional response to perceived risk. It often exceeds measured risk and can be shaped by media, local disorder and prior victimisation. Repeat victimisation means the same person, household or place is victimised again; the risk is highest soon after an incident. Near-repeat victimisation is a related pattern where nearby places or people are victimised soon after. Secondary victimisation is further harm caused by police, courts, media or health staff through insensitive treatment.

In a Nigerian case, after a burglary in Kaduna, Amina is burgled again within weeks and then questioned harshly at the station, so she stops reporting.

sections.heading: Rights and support
sections.text:
Victim rights and services vary by country. Common provisions include information, protection, compensation, restitution and the right to be heard.

The UN Declaration of Basic Principles of Justice for Victims of Crime and Abuse of Power (1985) is an international reference, not a binding world law. Support services include victim support schemes, shelters, counselling, legal advice and witness protection. They aim to reduce secondary harm and help recovery.

sections.heading: Victim surveys
sections.text:
Victim surveys ask a sample of people about crimes suffered, reported or not, and about fear and satisfaction with services.

Examples include the National Crime Victimization Survey in the United States and the Crime Survey for England and Wales. They reveal the dark figure of unreported crime but depend on memory, sampling and question design. They are not a count of all crime.

keyPoints: Victim typologies describe patterns of vulnerability or conduct and must not be used to blame victims.
Victims may report, testify and make impact statements, but their role varies by country.
Fear of crime often exceeds measured risk and is shaped by media, disorder and prior victimisation.
The risk of repeat victimisation is highest soon after an incident; secondary victimisation is harm caused by institutions.
Victim rights and support services vary by country; the 1985 UN Declaration is an international reference, not binding world law.
Victim surveys reveal unreported crime but depend on sampling, memory and question design.

en.title: Organised Crime and Illicit Markets
en.short: It covers definitions, trafficking, smuggling, money laundering, illicit markets, networks and enforcement cooperation.

sections.heading: Definitions and forms
sections.text: Definitions of organised crime vary by country. Criminologists often describe a continuing group that plans crimes, coordinates members and uses violence or corruption to profit. Legal definitions are narrower. Forms include illegal enterprises selling forbidden goods, protection networks, and groups that infiltrate legal business or public office. The UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, the Palermo Convention, requires states to criminalise participation in an organised criminal group and related offences.

sections.heading: Trafficking and smuggling
sections.text: Smuggling is the illegal movement of goods or people across a border; the migrant usually consents. Trafficking in persons involves recruiting, moving, harbouring or receiving a person by force, deception, fraud or abuse of power for exploitation. It can occur inside one country and needs no border crossing. The Palermo Protocol on Trafficking and the Protocol on Smuggling of Migrants are separate treaties. A smuggled person can later be trafficked, so investigators examine consent, coercion and exploitation, not movement alone.

sections.heading: Money laundering and flows
sections.text: Money laundering disguises the source of criminal proceeds so they appear lawful. Textbooks describe three stages: placement, layering and integration. Placement puts dirty money into the financial system; layering moves it through transactions to hide the trail; integration returns it as legitimate funds. Illicit financial flows are broader: money illegally earned, moved or used across borders. Financial Action Task Force (FATF) sets anti-money-laundering standards, applied in national law. Banks must identify customers and report suspicious transactions.

sections.heading: Markets, networks, enforcement
sections.text: Illegal markets arise where demand exists for goods or services that law forbids, such as stolen goods or protected wildlife. Criminal networks coordinate through trust and sometimes violence. Enforcement uses intelligence, financial investigation and asset recovery. Because crime crosses borders, police use Interpol, mutual legal assistance and extradition treaties. Suppose Tunde runs a Lagos haulage firm. He buys stolen fuel, trucks it across a border, and launders the cash through his firm’s takings at a bureau de change. This hypothetical case shows receiving stolen goods, smuggling, laundering and the need to trace fuel, money and evidence across borders.

keyPoints: Organised crime definitions vary by country, but criminologists stress continuing groups, planning and profit.
Smuggling involves illegal border crossing with consent; trafficking involves coercion or deception for exploitation and can occur within a country.
Money laundering has three common stages: placement, layering and integration.
Illicit financial flows are broader than laundering because they include money illegally earned, moved or used across borders.
Illegal markets and criminal networks rely on demand, trust, reputation and sometimes violence.
International cooperation includes the Palermo Convention, FATF standards, Interpol, mutual legal assistance and extradition.

en.title: Cybercrime and Digital Security
en.short: Types of cybercrime, offenders and victims, digital evidence, investigation basics, prevention and legal frameworks.

sections.heading: Types of cybercrime
sections.text: Cybercrime is crime involving computers or networks, either as target or tool. Online fraud is deception for money or property, such as fake sales. Phishing is tricking people into revealing passwords or card details through fake messages or websites. Identity theft is using another person’s personal data to impersonate them, often to obtain money or services. Cyberstalking is repeated unwanted contact or monitoring through digital channels that causes fear or distress. They overlap: phishing may lead to identity theft and fraud.

sections.heading: Offenders and victims
sections.text: Offenders range from lone opportunists to organised groups and insiders with legitimate access. Some actors are state-linked, but not all cybercrime is organised. Victims include individuals, firms and public bodies. Risk is shaped by exposure, security habits and vulnerability; victim blaming is unhelpful. A fictional case: Amina in Kano receives an SMS saying her bank account is blocked. A link asks for her PIN. She enters it, and money is moved. This is phishing leading to fraud. The bank’s logs and the message are evidence.

sections.heading: Evidence and investigation
sections.text: Digital evidence is information stored or transmitted in binary form that may prove a fact. It is fragile and easily altered. Investigators preserve it by isolating devices, documenting who handled what, making a forensic image (a bit-for-bit copy) and computing a hash (a digital fingerprint) to show integrity. A chain of custody records each transfer. Admissibility and search powers differ by country, so police need lawful authority and must respect privacy. Analysis links accounts, network logs, timestamps and devices, but attribution is difficult.

sections.heading: Prevention and law
sections.text: Prevention combines technical controls, such as multi-factor authentication (two or more different kinds of proof of identity), updates, encryption (scrambling data so only authorised users can read it) and backups, with awareness and organisational rules. Legal frameworks vary: Nigeria’s Cybercrimes Act 2015, the UK Computer Misuse Act 1990 and EU data protection law are examples, not universal standards. Students should check current national law. Digital security reduces risk; it cannot guarantee safety.

keyPoints: Cybercrime uses computers or networks as a target or as a tool.
Phishing tricks people into revealing data; identity theft uses data to impersonate.
Offenders range from lone opportunists to organised groups and insiders.
Digital evidence must be preserved, imaged and hashed, with a documented chain of custody.
Legal powers and admissibility vary by country; check current national law.
Prevention combines technical controls, awareness and regulation.

en.title: Terrorism, Political Violence and Counter-Terrorism
en.short: Contested definitions, causes, tactics, radicalisation, counter-terrorism and human rights safeguards.

sections.heading: Defining the terms
sections.text: Terrorism has no single agreed definition in law or scholarship. Many definitions combine four elements: violence or its threat, a political aim, civilians or non-combatants as targets, and the spread of fear. Disagreement remains over whether states can commit terrorism, whether armed groups are freedom fighters, and how much motive matters. Political violence is the wider category: violence used for political ends, including riots, repression, insurgency and genocide. Because labels carry moral and legal weight, define your terms before judging a case.

sections.heading: Causes and tactics
sections.text: Explanations are usually multi-causal. Grievances such as repression, inequality and injustice can supply motives; ideologies supply justifications; weak institutions and armed conflict supply opportunities. Tactics include bombings, armed attacks, hostage-taking, assassinations and, increasingly, cyber attacks and lone-actor violence. Groups choose tactics for visibility, cost, local support and state response. A tactic that provokes harsh repression can help a group recruit, so counter-terrorism design matters.

sections.heading: Radicalisation
sections.text: Radicalisation is the social process through which a person adopts extreme views that justify violence. It is not the same as terrorism: most radicalised people do not carry out attacks, and pathways vary. Push factors include identity grievances and state abuse; pull factors include group belonging, status and online networks. Research stresses contingency and relationships, not a single profile. Deradicalisation and reintegration programmes aim to reverse the process, but evidence on what works is mixed.

sections.heading: Counter-terrorism and rights
sections.text: Counter-terrorism includes policing, intelligence, military force, financial controls, border measures, prosecution and community programmes. Effective responses need legality, proportionality, due process and oversight. Harsh measures can alienate communities and reduce intelligence cooperation. Accountability means independent review of police and military action, remedies for victims, and fair trials. The 2014 Chibok abduction in Nigeria, by Boko Haram, shows how a mass atrocity can trigger security responses that also raise rights concerns; human rights bodies have documented abuses in such operations. Security and rights are not simple opposites: rights safeguards can build trust.

keyPoints: Terrorism has no single agreed legal or scholarly definition; many definitions combine political violence, civilian targets and fear.
Political violence is the broader category, and labels carry moral and legal consequences.
Causes are multi-causal: grievances and ideology supply motives, while weak institutions and conflict supply opportunities.
Radicalisation is a social process through which people adopt views that justify violence, but it does not always lead to terrorism.
Counter-terrorism should be lawful, proportionate and independently overseen.
Accountability requires fair trials, remedies for victims and review of police and military action.

en.title: Security Governance, Intelligence and Surveillance
en.short: National and human security, the intelligence cycle, surveillance, oversight and security sector reform.

sections.heading: Two ideas of security
sections.text:
National security protects the state: its sovereignty, territory and public order. Human security protects people: freedom from fear and want. The UNDP Human Development Report 1994 set out seven areas: economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community and political security.

The two aims can conflict. A mass arrest after a bombing may protect the state but reduce personal security. Good governance asks how to balance them openly.

sections.heading: Intelligence and surveillance
sections.text:
The intelligence cycle has five steps: planning and direction, collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination. Feedback then restarts it. Collection uses human sources, signals, images and open sources.

Surveillance is systematic watching of people or places. Data collection now includes metadata, which is information about a communication, not its content. Targeted surveillance focuses on a suspect; mass surveillance covers whole populations. Both need legal authority, necessity and proportionality.

sections.heading: Oversight and accountability
sections.text:
Oversight means checking security agencies. Internal oversight includes inspectors and audits. External oversight includes legislatures, courts, data protection authorities, media and civil society.

Accountability has two parts: answerability, explaining what was done, and consequences for wrongdoing. Secrecy is sometimes necessary, but it weakens oversight. The United Kingdom has an Investigatory Powers Commissioner who reviews certain surveillance. Laws differ by country, so students should check the current national framework.

sections.heading: Reform and civil-military relations
sections.text:
Security sector reform (SSR) seeks security forces that are effective, accountable and affordable. It covers police, military, intelligence, courts and prisons. Civil-military relations concern how elected civilians control the armed forces: roles, budgets, promotions and deployment.

Suppose Amina is a federal legislator in Nigeria. Soldiers are running roadblocks and taking cash. She can ask the defence committee to clarify the military’s role, require a published budget and refer extortion cases to the police and courts. That is SSR in practice.

keyPoints: National security protects the state; human security protects people’s freedom from fear and want.
The intelligence cycle runs from planning and direction through collection, processing, analysis and dissemination.
Surveillance and data collection must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.
Oversight can be internal or external, and accountability requires both explanation and consequences.
Security sector reform aims for effective, accountable and affordable security forces.
Civilian control means elected authorities set the roles, budgets and limits of the armed forces.

en.title: Research Design and Data Analysis in Criminology
en.short: Designing criminological studies: questions, sampling, measurement, analysis, ethics and writing up.

sections.heading: From question to design
sections.text: A criminological study starts with a clear, answerable research question, not a broad topic.
